correctness.rationale: Cells correspond to simple bipartite edges. A base degree at least three makes a triangle in the induced line graph; with maximum base degree two the base components are paths, even cycles and isolates, so the induced line graph is bipartite. The product of the two unsaturated sets must consist wholly of selected edges for maximality. When both are nonempty, each vertex there has degree at most one, so they are singletons joined by an isolated edge. Both degree sums are then one less than twice their shore sizes, forcing a square. Otherwise a shore is saturated; edge capacity makes it the smaller shore on rectangles and both shores on squares. These criteria are sufficient too. In the saturated classes only isolated larger-shore vertices, alternating paths with one extra larger-shore vertex and even cycles occur. Dividing alternating list counts by orientation and, for cycles, label starting position gives k!(k+1)!/2 and (k!)²/(2k). The resulting labeled EGF is g(xy)exp(y h(xy)); exactly n−m factors carrying an extra y gives the stated coefficient. The other square class amounts to choosing the two isolated-edge endpoints and a two-factor on the remaining labels. A two-factor on one row and one column is impossible, while spanning even cycles realize both sizes for n≥3; a single alternating path on all rows and m+1 columns realizes the rectangular size. Independent direct two-coloring and single-cell extension tests agree with all five checked polynomials.
residual_risks: Independent exhaustive checks cover 2×2, 3×3, 3×4, 3×5 and 4×4. The unrestricted result relies on the structural proof and exact coefficient extraction, not those data.

evidence: Reiner–Roberts treat rational homology for capacity-bounded complexes. Multiple chessboard complexes are defined with both capacities, while the inspected symmetric-family treatment then specializes to column capacity one.

Singh's balanced capacity n−1 homotopy-sphere theorem has capacity two only at n=3. The Jojić et al. 2020 abstract describes a connectivity result for multiplicity chessboard complexes, without an all-board facet formula in the material read.
broader_coverage.reasoning: A homotopy or homology computation does not determine how many inclusion-maximal faces occur at each size. The cited balanced capacity theorem does not include strict rectangles or the fixed-capacity-two regime at larger n, and one-column-capacity cases are not the same family.

evidence: Removing the three-star terms from the earlier all-set generating function gives the degree-two all-face generating function. Its top rectangular size coefficient already supplies the number of faces of size 2m, and its square two-factor coefficient is explicitly given.
The prior maximal-forest purity result concerns linear forests (no cycles); Hamilton paths on square boards can be closed to even cycles, so maximal forests there need not be maximal bipartite sets.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The rectangular top coefficient becomes the full facet census only after proving that no smaller maximal faces exist. On squares, a face of size 2n−1 could be an extendible spanning path or an isolated edge plus cycles. The prior two-factor enumeration makes the smaller facet count immediate once the isolated-edge classification is known, but it does not identify the maximal subcollection. The new content is the general unsaturated-pair criterion applied to facets, with its full polynomial and purity consequences, not a claim to invent the component EGF.

evidence: Known bounded-degree or multiple chessboard complexes constrain row and column occupancy, so the capacity-(2,2) case is the same admissible-set complex. Singh defines exactly the degree-at-most-r edge complex.
The earlier indexed three-independence result allows the additional connected base component K_{1,3}; the corresponding line graph triangle makes it inadmissible here.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: For the line graph of a bipartite base, being induced triangle-free, bipartite, or represented by a degree-two matching all specify the same feasible sets. These are aliases, not separate contributions. Induced rook maximum-degree two is a distinct property and its extra components may affect maximality.

exact_database_or_table.reasoning: Inclusion-maximal (not merely maximum) is crucial: neither the indexed all-square top coefficient nor the finite face counts give a general census of smaller facets. A face census on finitely many boards cannot imply the sharp all-parameter transition.

originality.rationale: The supported distinct finding is the complete inclusion-maximal facet classification and enumerator, in particular the rectangular purity versus square nonpurity transition and exact contribution of smaller square facets. The larger square coefficient B_n and finite-board entries are demonstrably prior, not separate new results. The prior path-and-cycle generating functions also supply ingredients for the rectangular top coefficient. Neither those ingredients nor the strongest inspected homology and enumeration results give the inclusion-maximal classification at all parameters.
residual_risks: The comparison does not establish absolute publication priority. An unindexed thesis, another bounded-degree matching treatment, or a passage not assessed in the general chessboard literature might contain the facet classification. The 2020 discrete-Morse paper was not assessed in full. Neither limited access nor a search miss establishes absence.

value.rationale: The classification locates exactly when all inclusion-maximal bipartite choices on the natural rook graph are optimal and when a second facet dimension occurs. The nonmaximum square class gives genuinely useful facet data that an ordinary face enumerator or top-coefficient census does not isolate. Having the combined size distribution and its sharp shape criterion for the degree-two chessboard complex is a meaningful exact result; the individual already-known top counts are not its contribution.
residual_risks: Facet purity and counts do not establish shellability, Cohen–Macaulayness, or any specific homotopy type.
